Date: Sep 16, 2025 Tags: NIST CSF, Network Security, Forensics, MonitoringLaws mandates organizations to adopt structured cybersecurity frameworks to meet legal obligations.US federal law that aims to improve cybersecurity through public-private partnership, enhance research and development, and promote workforce education and awareness. Also known as Public Law No: 113-274Titled Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, issued on Feb 2013 due to increasing cyber threats to critical infrastructure. It focuses on three areas: information sharing privacy adoption of cybersecurity practices National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) was directed to develop a cybersecurity framework from existing voluntary consensus standards and industry best practices. Titled Strengthening the Cybersecurity of Federal Networks and Critical Infrastructure, issued on May 2017. Mandates the framework for all government agencies Still voluntary for everyone else Requires agencies to: Inventory computer systems Identify and provide appropriate security protections Develop, document, and implement agency-wide information security program Intended to reduce cracking of computer systems and to address federal computer-related offenses. Mainly for financial and government computer systems but later include civilians' computer and even cellphones.Extended the restrictions on wire taps and other electronic communications in transit Protects stored electronic communication Added pen/traps provisions that permits tracking of telephone communications (with court order)Now covers personal identifiable information (PII) Restrict disclosure Increase right of access to agency records Grant individuals the right to seek amendment Establish a code of fair information practices
[Executive Order on Strengthening the Cybersecurity of Federal Networks and Critical Infrastructure | CISA]

projects/turning-32-bit-laptop-into-an-n.title: Turning 32-bit laptop into an nftables Firewall
projects/turning-32-bit-laptop-into-an-n.description:
Date: Jun 14, 2026 Tags: Network Security System Administration Hardware Troubleshooting Firewall DNS Sinkhole Log Management Linux nftables rsyslog { "type": "project", "spec": [ { "name": "cybersecurity", "rank": 9, "description": "Repurposed a retired 32-bit laptop into a Linux-based firewall for a small cybersecurity lab. Using AntiX Linux, nftables, dnsmasq, rsyslog, and logrotate, the firewall provides network address translation (NAT), stateful packet filtering, DNS sinkholing, and centralized logging." }, { "name": "it-support", "rank": 7, "description": "Extended the usability of legacy 32-bit laptop by upgrading hardware components, installing a lightweight operating system, and configuring the device as a firewall host." } ] } Project Summary This project repurposed a retired 32-bit laptop into a Linux-based firewall for a small cybersecurity lab. Using AntiX Linux, nftables, dnsmasq, rsyslog, and logrotate, the firewall provides network address translation (NAT), stateful packet filtering, DNS sinkholing, and centralized logging. The implementation was validated through connectivity, domain-blocking, and traffic-filtering tests while addressing challenges associated with aging hardware and limited resources.
Firewall is one of the most common and crucial defenses for network security. It controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predefined rules. Due to limited resources, I am using an old laptop running on 32-bit AntiX Linux. The firewall will use the nftables, the default backend firewall of Linux. Configure network configuration for the AntiX Linux. Configure AntiX Linux as a nftables firewall and DNS sinkhole. Configure Log rotation. Configure Lab Router for the lab. Apply, test, and verify basic firewall rules. Figure 1 shows the network diagram for this entry. The firewall will use nftables for Network Address Translation and filtering on the network and transport layer. While dnsmasq is used for DNS sinkholing in the application layer. The Lab router will bridge the lab hosts to external networks.
Figure 1: Network diagramSoftware and Hardware components used: Installed AntiX Linux with atleast 2 Network Interface Cards (NIC). SSH enabled on AntiX for remote management. I start by renaming the laptop's interfaces. Rationale By setting the interface names to something more intuitive like lan0 and wan0, it will be easier for the future to manage, test, and troubleshooting in the future.
Renaming wan0 and lan0 interface I first identified the MAC Addresses of the interface with ip addr, then changed their NAME= on /etc/udev/rules.d/70-persistent-net.rules. Then, I configured the network interfaces. To make IP addresses easier to distinguish, and given that wan0 is on 192.168.11.0/24. I set lan0 interface to 173.16.0.0/24 and intended to use 10.0.0.0/24 for the lab. Figure 2 shows the current network connection on the firewall host. Network interface configuration In line 12-15, I set the lan0 to 172.168.0.1/24, it is important that the interface connected to this is also on the same network. In line 18-27, wan0 I set the static IP address of the firewall host to 192.168.11.200, setting static IP on servers and network hosts helps with accessibility and reduce configuration errors. In line 30, I added a route to LabNetwork (10.0.0.0/24) via firwall's lan0 (172.16.0.1) interface was specified. Without this, traffic going to 10.0.0.0/24 will be forwarded to 192.168.11.1 (gateway). ... 7 8 auto lo 9 iface lo inet loopback 10 11 # LAN - (Ethernet) 12 auto lan0 13 iface lan0 inet static 14 address 172.16.0.1 15 netmask 255.255.255.0 16 17 # WAN (Wireless) 18 auto wan0 19 iface wan0 inet static 20 address 192.168.11.200 21 netmask 255.255.255.0 22 gateway 192.168.11.1 23 dns-nameservers 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4 24 25 26 27 wpa-conf /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf 28 29 # Route to LAB network 30 up ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.2 dev lan0
Figure 2: Network connection and routing table on firewall host (AntiX Linux). I enabled IP forwarding and Network Address Translation (NAT) on the firewall. Rationale The default policy on all chains for table inet filter was set to drop following a Zero Trust approach where all connections are denied unless explicitly allowed. Initial nftables firewall config The logging prefix on my config will follow the pattern NFT-[CHAIN]-[ACTION]-[KEYWORD] to make logs easier to analyze and because the action is not included on nftables logs by default. 1 flush ruleset 2 3 table inet filter { 4 chain input { 5 type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop; 6 iif "lo" accept 7 ct state established,related accept 8 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-IN-DROP-INVALID " drop 9 ip saddr 10.0.0.50 tcp dport 22 accept 10 tcp dport 53 accept 11 udp dport 53 accept 12 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 13 log prefix "NFT-IN-DROP-DEFAULT " 14 } 15 16 chain forward { 17 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; 18 ct state established,related accept 19 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-INVALID " drop 20 ip daddr 9.9.9.9 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-QUAD9 " drop 21 tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept 22 udp dport { 53, 123 } accept 23 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 24 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-DEFAULT " 25 } 26 27 chain output { 28 type filter hook output priority filter; policy drop; 29 ct state established,related accept 30 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-OUT-DROP-INVALID " drop 31 hour "17:00"-"04:00" tcp dport { 80, 443, 53 } log prefix "NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC " accept 32 hour "17:00"-"04:00" udp dport { 53, 123 } log prefix "NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC " accept 33 tcp dport { 53, 80, 443 } accept 34 udp dport { 53, 123 } accept 35 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 36 log prefix "NFT-OUT-DROP-DEFAULT " 37 } 38 } 39 table ip nat { 40 chain prerouting { 41 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; 42 iifname "lan0" udp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 43 iifname "lan0" tcp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 44 } 45 46 chain postrouting { 47 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; 48 oifname "wan0" masquerade 49 } 50 } Since nftables is filtering on the OSI network layer (L3) and transport layer (L4). I also added a DNS Sinkhole using dnsmasq to filter domains. In Figure 7, I blocked the domain chess.com for testing purposes. 1 # DNS sinkhole list 2 address=/chess.com/ Figure 3: List of domain names blocked on /etc/dnsmasq.d/blocklist.conf. Lastly, I set up the logging mechanism on rsyslog using the config on Figure 4. This creates dedicated log files to store firewall logs. The $syslogtag was set by using imfile on rsyslog.conf. 1 # 1. Capture Firewall logs 2 :msg, contains, "NFT-" /var/log/nftables.log 3 & stop 4 5 # 2. Capture DNS queries 6 if ($syslogtag == 'dnsmasq_log') then { 7 /var/log/dns.log 8 stop 9 } 10 Figure 4: 1. All logs that has string that has "NFT-" will be stored on /var/log/nftables.log. 2. All dnsmasq_log will be stored on /var/log/dns.logImporting imfile module on rsyslog.conf This gives rsyslog access to dnsmasq.log to add tag=dnsmasq_log # <Redacted> 23 module(load="imfile") 24 25 input(type="imfile" 26 File="/var/log/dnsmasq.log" 27 Tag="dnsmasq_log" 28 Severity="info" 29 Facility="local0") # <Redacted> I created a logrotate config that keeps logs in manageable size. Since dns.log would certainly contain a lot more logs, I set the frequency to daily and only store up to 7 log archives at once.
Figure 5 Log rotation config on /etc/logrotate.d/firewall. I set the network configuration first by following Figure 6 and Figure 7. Figure 6: Lab router's WAN configuration. Figure 7: Lab router's LAN configuration. Then, I disabled Network Address Translation (NAT) on the lab router. Architecture The router will now forward traffic to its default gateway (firewall's lan0 interface) without changing the source IP addresses. With the placement of the firewall, disabling NAT on the edge router allows the firewall to see internal IP addresses which gives more control and insights over the traffic coming in and out of the lab.
Figure 8: NAT was disabled on the lab router. I applied the nftables rules and for the dnsmasq using the command below. sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf sudo service dnsmasq restart sudo service rsyslog restart Figure 9: Apply the nftables.conf rules and restart dnsmasq and rsyslog service. I connected to the LabNetwork and tested the created rules. Based on the test summary (see Figure 10), the nftables and dnsmasq implementation is working as expected. Figure 10. Test SummaryInput Chain Tests A. SSH - External host connecting to firewall via SSH nftables log: 2026-06-17T19:02:30.790210+08:00 firewall kernel: [ 948.929678] NFT-IN-DROP-DEFAULT IN=wan0 OUT= MAC=00:13:02:2e:1f:c9:d6:6b:98:02:e7:74:08:00 SRC=192.168.11.183 DST=192.168.11.200 LEN=60 TOS=0x18 PREC=0xA0 TTL=64 ID=54929 DF PROTO=TCP SPT=49080 DPT=22 WINDOW=65535 RES=0x00 SYN URGP= B. SSH - Lab host (.100) connecting to firewall via SSH nftables log: 2026-06-17T19:28:53.751939+08:00 firewall kernel: [ 2531.891358] NFT-IN-DROP-DEFAULT IN=lan0 OUT= MAC=00:03:0d:53:17:49:30:16:9d:72:51:2b:08:00 SRC=10.0.0.100 DST=172.16.0.1 LEN=60 TOS=0x00 PREC=0x00 TTL=63 ID=14874 DF PROTO=TCP SPT=43002 DPT=22 WINDOW=65535 RES=0x00 SYN URGP=0 C. DNS Lookup using the firewall output: Server: UnKnown Address: 172.16.0.1 Non-authoritative answer: Name: jamilosa.com Addresses: 185.199.108.153 185.199.110.153 185.199.111.153 185.199.109.153 Forward Chain Tests A. Lab host connecting to am external SSH server nftables log: 2026-06-17T19:32:51.174478+08:00 firewall kernel: [ 2769.313896] NFT-FOR-DROP-DEFAULT IN=lan0 OUT=wan0 MAC=00:03:0d:53:17:49:30:16:9d:72:51:2b:08:00 SRC=10.0.0.100 DST=192.168.1.1 LEN=60 TOS=0x18 PREC=0xA0 TTL=62 ID=30969 DF PROTO=TCP SPT=41394 DPT=22 WINDOW=65535 RES=0x00 SYN URGP=0 B. Lab host connecting to an external host via port 8080 nftables log: 2026-06-17T19:35:10.349186+08:00 firewall kernel: [ 2908.488607] NFT-FOR-DROP-DEFAULT IN=lan0 OUT=wan0 MAC=00:03:0d:53:17:49:30:16:9d:72:51:2b:08:00 SRC=10.0.0.100 DST=192.168.1.1 LEN=60 TOS=0x00 PREC=0x00 TTL=62 ID=24723 DF PROTO=TCP SPT=43256 DPT=8080 WINDOW=65535 RES=0x00 SYN URGP=0 C. Lab host pings external host jamilosa.com output: Reply from 185.199.110.153: bytes=32 time=13ms TTL=56 Reply from 185.199.110.153: bytes=32 time=16ms TTL=56 Reply from 185.199.110.153: bytes=32 time=12ms TTL=56 Reply from 185.199.110.153: bytes=32 time=19ms TTL=56 Output Chain Tests A. Firewall host connecting to external IP on allowed port 443 output:
nftables log: 2026-06-17T19:39:10.794366+08:00 firewall kernel: [ 3148.933773] NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC IN= OUT=wan0 SRC=192.168.11.200 DST=192.168.1.1 LEN=60 TOS=0x00 PREC=0x00 TTL=64 ID=3067 DF PROTO=TCP SPT=58604 DPT=443 WINDOW=64240 RES=0x00 SYN URGP=0 DNS Sinkhole Tests A. Accessing blocked domain chess.com
output: $ nslookup chess.com Server: UnKnown Address: 172.16.0.1 *** UnKnown can't find chess.com: No response from server dns log: 2026-06-17T21:05:27.351505+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: query[A] chess.com from 10.0.0.50 2026-06-17T21:05:27.351547+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: config chess.com is NXDOMAIN 2026-06-17T21:05:27.354389+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: query[AAAA] chess.com from 10.0.0.50 2026-06-17T21:05:27.354447+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: config chess.com is NXDOMAIN
The internet connection on the lab network (firewall's wan0 interface) is really slow. The wireless adaptor only supports 802.11a/g standards which can theoretically handle only up to 54Mbps. This is the bottleneck is in terms of connection speed for the lab. dns.log and nftables.log have different log formats. This is likely true for a lot of applications and services. In order to properly parse them on the SIEM, I need to use different decoders. nftables is mainly for filtering Layer 3 (Network) and Layer 4 (Transport) traffic. It can also act as a stateful firewall. For blocking domains, using IP ranges could potentially cause inconvenience and holes on the network. Many modern websites are being delivered or tunneled via the massive IP blocks of companies like Cloudflare. DNS Sinkholing solves this specific problem. Devices generate a lot of DNS query. While it might be useful to log for correlation and attack mapping, it will also be accompanied with a lot of noise. I tried triggering a firewall drop rule and the log shows it was triggered on a different time. The longer the inaccuracy on the time, the more it would be confusing to correlate them especially across multiple hosts. This shows the importance of synchronized time across systems. Setup Wazuh server for centralized log collection and to monitor lab hosts. Update firewall rules for better security. Setup windows server and vulnerable hosts inside the lab. Attack the vulnerable hosts inside the lab This project successfully turned and old 32-bit laptop into a functioning firewall for my simple cybersecurity lab. It provided network address translation, network and transport layer filtering, along with stateful filtering using nftables. It also functions as dns sinkhole for blocking domains using dnsmasq. Logs are recorded on the firewall for log correlation and analysis. The logs are also rotated to prevent storage issues.While working in this project, I realized the limitations of L3/L4 firewalls in network security. That's why I added domain sinkholing on the go to try and imitate the basic network security capabilites most real world corporate network have. I also learned the critical value of syncing time across systems as it is one of the fields used for correlation.In the next entries, I would setup a Wazuh server that will store logs of lab hosts. Having a centralized place to view and correlate logs would make it easier to discover anomalies on the network. I will also install and attack a windows server and vulnerable hosts in the lab.
